You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: What the failing test does
- It integrates a simple exponential system from a very large absolute time t0 = 1878250320.0000029 to an “end event” time tEvent = 1878250379.9999986 (intended duration ≈ 60 s) using a fixed-step ClassicalRungeKuttaIntegrator with step size 60.0.
- It expects the integrator to stop at tEvent (within 5e-6).

How end-of-range is implemented
- The base integrator injects an artificial event via addEndTimeChecker(t0, tEvent, eventsHandlersManager), which adds an EndTimeChecker(endTime) into a CombinedEventsManager.
- EndTimeChecker’s event function g(t, y) is effectively “distance to end time” (e.g., g(t) = t − endTime), and when it is detected crossing zero, the integration should stop.
- The convergence used for locating the event is set to Math.ulp(max(|t0|, |tEvent|)), which here is about 4e-7 due to the large absolute magnitude of the times.

Where the bug is triggered
- The main stepping loop in RungeKuttaIntegrator.integrate(...) computes a trial end-of-step and asks the CombinedEventsManager to detect events across that step (manager.evaluateStep(interpolator)).
- If an event is detected, the code computes dt = manager.getEventTime() − stepStart and then:
  - If |dt| > Math.ulp(stepStart), it truncates the step to align exactly with the event (stepSize = dt).
  - If |dt| <= Math.ulp(stepStart), it follows a “special case” branch that sets loop = false with the comment “we set up an artificial 0 size step,” but it does not actually adjust the step size or the step end time.

Why it goes past the end time
- In this test, with large absolute times and a 60 s step, the first step generally detects the end event inside the step and truncates close to tEvent (difference within a few microseconds).
- After that truncated acceptance, due to floating-point rounding the next step start is within about one ulp of the event time. On the very next iteration, manager.evaluateStep(interpolator) can report another event at dt ≲ ulp(stepStart), which triggers the “tiny dt” branch.
- In that branch, the code intends to handle an “artificial 0-size step” but does not actually set the step to zero or advance to the event time. It just breaks the inner loop without modifying stepSize. Immediately afterward, the method accepts the step and computes nextStep = stepStart + stepSize.
- Critically, stepSize has been reset to the default fixed step (60.0) just before starting the new step (the code sets stepSize = forward ? step : -step after each accepted step). Therefore, instead of performing a 0-size step at the event, the integrator advances by a full 60 s beyond the end time, effectively skipping the stopping event.
- Once it has skipped past the event in this way, the end event may be missed again in subsequent steps (depending on sign and bracketing logic), yielding a final integration span that overshoots well beyond the intended 60 s. The issue report mentions a 160 s total span, which matches the behavior of accepting one or more full 60 s steps past the target because the tiny-dt branch prevents proper alignment and stopping.

Key code responsible (from RungeKuttaIntegrator.integrate)
- Event handling section:
  - manager.evaluateStep(interpolator)
  - dt = manager.getEventTime() − stepStart
  - if (Math.abs(dt) <= Math.ulp(stepStart)) { loop = false; } else { stepSize = dt; }
- After the loop:
  - nextStep = stepStart + stepSize; ...
  - stepSize is reset to the default fixed step after each accepted step.

Root cause
- The “tiny-dt” branch incorrectly claims to set up an artificial 0-size step but does not adjust the step end or step size. Combined with the unconditional reset of stepSize to the default 60 s, this causes the integrator to accept a full step and skip over the end-of-range event whenever the remaining time to the event is within one ulp of the current step start. This is exactly the “numerical accuracy in events detection leads to error in events location” described in the bug report and explains why the integration runs past the specified end of the integration range.

Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
